hook: Chemistry's center of gravity moved France → Germany → the US: the US overtook Germany among chemists born in the 1860s and peaked at 41% of everyone born in the 1910s.
caveat: English-Wikipedia notability over-represents anglophone chemists; shares are of notable chemists, not of all chemists.

hook: The US is chemistry's great talent magnet: a net gain of 482 migrant chemists, with Germany → the US the single busiest corridor (70 people); the biggest net exporters are Germany, Austria, Russia.
caveat: Direction comes from place of birth vs. citizenship; moves without naturalisation are invisible.

hook: Chemists born in 1900–1929 reached a median age of 86, versus 69 for those born in the 1700s; chemists who held more than one citizenship had a 18% lower hazard of death (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.74–0.91).
caveat: Survivorship bias: you must live long enough to become notable. Medians describe notable chemists, not mortality in the general population; living people are right-censored.

hook: Academic family trees run deep: 495 of the 2,372 chemists with recorded advisor links (21%) belong to a single advisor-to-student lineage whose earliest recorded root is Vittorino da Feltre (b. 1378); the academic descendants of Daniel Sennert (b. 1572) include 65 Nobel laureates.
caveat: Only advisor links recorded in Wikidata (P184/P185); coverage is sparse and skews to famous labs.

hook: Women are 36% of chemists born since 1960 in Wikidata, up from 7.2% of those born before 1900. Even at today's rate, notable chemistry is still roughly 2 men to every woman.
caveat: Sex/gender as recorded in Wikidata (P21). Recognition gaps in Wikipedia itself depress women's counts.

hook: Chemistry turned toward life: biochemists, pharmacologists and toxicologists were 14% of chemists born in 1850–1879 but 35% of those born in 1940–1969.
caveat: Many people carry only the generic 'chemist' label, so specialty shares are lower bounds.
